**TASK: Mega Menu UX Research — 3 levels deep**

Delegate this to Probe (your UX subordinate). Do not do it alone.

**Context:**
- We have a navigation with 11 top-level categories: Boots, Multi-Stud Boots, Indoor Shoes, Shin Guards, Balls, Socks, Jerseys, Kits, Apparel, Clothing, Accessories
- The category tree is: Category > Brand > Model > Sub-model > Product Type
- **Only 3 levels show in the mega menu:** Category, Brand, Model
- Sub-models and product types show as filters on the category page

**Rules for the mega menu:**
- Each column is ONE category with its brands and models nested underneath
- NOT one column for categories, one for brands, one for models
- So Boots column shows: Adidas > Predator, X, F50 | Nike > Mercurial, Phantom | Puma > Future, Ultra
- Only 3 levels deep max

**First: Read our current mega menu implementation**
- Read `src/components/navigation/MegaMenu.tsx` or wherever the mega menu component is
- Read `data/navigation.json` — see how the current mega menu is structured
- Understand what it looks like now

**Then research:**
1. Look at Nike.com, Adidas.com, Decathlon, Foot Locker, JD Sports — how do they show 3 levels of hierarchy in their mega menu? Each category column with brands and models nested inside?

2. Find the best way to present this without overwhelming customers with 11 columns. Some ideas:
   - Group smaller categories into "More" dropdown
   - Show featured/popular categories only, with "View All" link
   - Show brand logos instead of text

3. Mobile: How should 3-level navigation work on mobile?

**Return:**
- Analysis of our current mega menu
- Examples from real sites showing the "category column with nested brands/models" pattern
- Recommended design for Athletica (desktop + mobile)
- Wireframe description of the final design

The user (likely Hermes, my superior) is giving me a task to delegate to Probe. This is a research task about mega menu UX. Let me follow my startup procedure first.

Let me check my status files and the project structure to understand what's going on.

27: #### Levels Visible

36:   - Column 1: "New & Featured" (curated links: New Releases, Best Sellers, Latest Drops)

39:   - Column 4 (optional): "Accessories & Equipment" and/or promotional image block

46: - **On category pages:** Nike uses a "pictoral menu" — horizontal row of category tiles WITH images at the top of the PLP (per econsultancy.com)

49: - **Desktop:** Hover-triggered with short intent delay (~200-300ms) per thehangline.com and fatcowwebdesign.com

51: - **Close behavior:** Panel closes on mouse-leave. Recommended 150ms close delay prevents accidental closure

55: - **Nike's approach:** Mega menu intentionally avoids deep hierarchies. Only 2 levels max in the panel.

152: #### Column Layout
153: - **Mega menu is NOT used in the traditional sense.** Decathlon uses a search-navigation hybrid approach instead of a classic mega menu.

# Mega Menu UX Research — Comprehensive Report for Athletica (Part 1: Site Analysis — Nike, Adidas, Decathlon)

> **Compiled by:** Probe-Orion (Intelligence Team)
> **Task:** task-mega-menu-ux-001
> **Date:** 2026-07-19
> **Purpose:** Final comprehensive synthesis of all research inputs to inform Athletica's mega menu design for a 5-level hierarchy (Category → Brand → Model → Sub-model → Product Type)
> **Input sources:** Probe-Orion (Nike/Adidas), Probe-Wren (Decathlon/Foot Locker/JD Sports), Probe-Beacon (ASOS/Zalando), Probe-Sable (Deep Hierarchy Part A & B)

---

## Table of Contents (All Parts)

- **Part 1:** Site Analysis — Nike, Adidas, Decathlon [THIS FILE]
- **Part 2:** Site Analysis — Foot Locker, JD Sports, ASOS, Zalando + Cross-Site Comparison Tables
- **Part 3:** Best Practices for Deep Hierarchies (Desktop)
- **Part 4:** Mobile Strategy
- **Part 5:** Athletica-Specific Recommendations + Sources Cited

---

## Section 1: Site Analysis

### 1.1 Nike.com

**Source:** Probe-Orion research, `megamenu-nike-adidas.md`

#### Levels Visible
- **Top-level nav items:** ~6 primary links: "New & Featured", "Men", "Women", "Kids", "Jordan", "Sale" (per styles.refero.design — structure identical across locales)
- **Visible within mega menu panel:** 2 levels only — bold category headings (not clickable) with subcategory links below them
- **Not shown:** Levels 3+ are NOT exposed inside the mega menu. Users must click through to a category page to see deeper levels.
- **On category pages:** Nike adds a nested left-hand sidebar menu above the filters showing the current category hierarchy (per econsultancy.com comparison)

#### Column Layout
- **3–5 columns** per panel (per thehangline.com; styles.refero.design)
- **Column distribution (Men/Women/Kids identical structure):**
  - Column 1: "New & Featured" (curated links: New Releases, Best Sellers, Latest Drops)
  - Column 2: "Shoes" (subcategories: Lifestyle, Running, Basketball, Football, Training & Gym)
  - Column 3: "Clothing" (subcategories: Tops & T-Shirts, Shorts, Hoodies, Jackets)
  - Column 4 (optional): "Accessories & Equipment" and/or promotional image block
- **White background,** full-width panel, no border/shadow on the nav bar (per styles.refero.design)
- **Typography:** Column headings bold, 14-16px; link text regular weight, slightly smaller (per thehangline.com)

#### Images/Thumbnails
- **NO product thumbnails, category images, or icons** inside the menu columns (per unlimited-elements.com — "No images. It focuses on simplicity"; wpmet.com — "No distracting icons")
- **Promotional image on the right side** — optional one-column-wide promotional banner (per thehangline.com)
- **On category pages:** Nike uses a "pictoral menu" — horizontal row of category tiles WITH images at the top of the PLP (per econsultancy.com)

#### Hover vs Click
- **Desktop:** Hover-triggered with short intent delay (~200-300ms) per thehangline.com and fatcowwebdesign.com
- **Click also supported** — clicking a top-level nav item also opens the panel (accessibility requirement)
- **Close behavior:** Panel closes on mouse-leave. Recommended 150ms close delay prevents accidental closure
- **Keyboard:** Tab → navigates items, Enter/Space → open/close, Escape → close (per fatcowwebdesign.com)

#### Deep Category Handling
- **Nike's approach:** Mega menu intentionally avoids deep hierarchies. Only 2 levels max in the panel.
- **For deeper navigation (3+ levels):**
  1. User clicks a subcategory link (e.g., "Football" under "Shoes") → loads a category page
  2. Category page has a nested left-hand sidebar showing the current category and all sibling subcategories (per econsultancy.com)
  3. Category page also features a "pictoral menu" with images for visual browsing
  4. Further filters (nested left, sticky) handle remaining refinement
- **Philosophy:** Mega menu as a broad funnel, category page navigation for deep drilling. Kept intentionally shallow to avoid choice paralysis (per katsaville.com — "Editing — Help users to navigate without choice paralysis or overwhelm")

#### Distinctive Patterns
1. **Audience-first navigation** — Primary split by audience (Men/Women/Kids) rather than by product type (per exclusiveaddons.com, wpmet.com)
2. **Text-only minimalist design** — No imagery inside the menu panel. Relies on typographic hierarchy and white space (per unlimited-elements.com)
3. **Consistent structure across sections** — Every audience section uses the same column layout (per katsaville.com)
4. **"New & Featured" as first column** — Blends marketing content with navigation (per exclusiveaddons.com, katsaville.com)
5. **No sticky header** — Nav bar is NOT sticky, sits on white background with no fill/shadow/border (per styles.refero.design)
6. **Two-tier nav bar** — Thin utility bar (search, help, login) in 12px above main nav row (per styles.refero.design)
7. **Search field:** Background #f5f5f5, 24px border radius, placeholder in #707072 (per styles.refero.design)

#### Mobile Approach
- **Hamburger icon** opens a **full-screen overlay** (per muffingroup.com — "splits items into sections under visible headings")
- **Accordion-style expansion** — Tapping a top-level item expands inline to show subcategories (per muffingroup.com, nngroup.com/mobile-subnavigation/)
- **Staggered fade-in animation** — Items fade in ~50ms apart (per muffingroup.com)
- **4 main parent categories:** Men, Women, Kids, Nike by You (per uxdesign.cc)
- **No images in mobile nav** — Text-only accordion (per muffingroup.com)
- **Desktop structure translates** to simplified accordion format for mobile (per wpmet.com)

---

### 1.2 Adidas.com

**Source:** Probe-Orion research, `megamenu-nike-adidas.md`

#### Levels Visible
- **Top-level nav items:** 5 primary links: "MEN", "WOMEN", "KIDS", "Sale", "New & Trending" (per plerdy.com; confirmed via adidas.com)
- **Visible within mega menu panel:** 2 levels typically — category headings + subcategory links
- **Not shown:** Levels 3+ are NOT exposed in the mega menu. Users click through to category/subcategory pages for deeper refinement.
- **Refinement on category pages:** Robust filter systems (by price, discount, sport, product type) handle deep drilling (per econsultancy.com)

#### Column Layout
- **Multi-column layout** with gender-based categories (per wpmet.com)
- **Refined by two orthogonal dimensions:** "Product Type" (Shoes, Clothing, Accessories) AND "Sports" (Running, Football, Training, Basketball, etc.) (per wpmet.com)
- **Distinctive BOTTOM ROW** — Full-width bottom section with additional links, "View All" options (per wpmet.com — "includes the bottom row for further information")
- **Column distribution (estimated):**
  - Columns for product types (Shoes, Clothing, Accessories)
  - Columns for sports categories
  - Bottom row: "View All" links, featured content
  - Right-side or interspersed: promotional images/banners
- **High-contrast design elements** with bold typography (per wpmet.com)

#### Images/Thumbnails
- **YES — Adidas uses images extensively** in the mega menu (per wpmet.com — "Visual Storytelling: Uses promotional images to highlight offers and collaborations")
- **Promotional banners** for seasonal campaigns, collaborations (per wpmet.com)
- **Category thumbnail images** — The "brands menu" contains thumbnail images for each brand (per econsultancy.com)
- **Large product shots** within the menu for featured/new items (per rsacreativestudio.com)
- **Fast-loading visual assets** — optimized for performance within navigation (per wpmet.com)

#### Hover vs Click
- **Desktop:** Hover-triggered with intent delay (~200-300ms) per industry standard
- **Click also supported** for keyboard and touch accessibility
- **Close:** Panel dismisses on mouse-leave with a forgiveness delay

#### Deep Category Handling
- **Adidas approach:** Like Nike, the mega menu shows max 2 levels.
- **For deeper navigation:**
  1. User clicks a subcategory (e.g., "Shoes" under "Men") → goes to category page
  2. Category pages use robust filter panels (by sport, price, discount, size, color) for deeper refinement
  3. Category pages feature a "category grid" with product thumbnails and "Shop Now" CTAs (per mobbin.com)
- **Key difference from Nike:** Adidas does NOT have the nested left-hand sidebar menu on category pages (per econsultancy.com — "the lack of that nested menu... is the most annoying")
- **"Many routes in" approach** — More paths to find products: by sport, by product type, by brand, by color, by collection (per econsultancy.com)

#### Distinctive Patterns
1. **Image-heavy mega menu** — Promotional images, product shots, category thumbnails within the menu (per wpmet.com, rsacreativestudio.com)
2. **Bottom row in mega menu** — Full-width bottom section with additional links/CTAs (per wpmet.com)
3. **"Shop By Color" submenu** — Allows browsing by color directly from navigation (per wpmet.com)
4. **Sport-specific sub-categories** — Organizes by sport (Running, Football, Training, Basketball) as a first-class dimension (per wpmet.com)
5. **Bold, large typography** — Large sans-serif fonts, highly readable (per wpmet.com)
6. **Dynamic "New & Trending" sections** — Frequently updated to drive engagement (per wpmet.com)
7. **"All" category links in bold** — Bold "All" links at the bottom of each submenu (per econsultancy.com)
8. **Dual dimension navigation** — Browse by "Product Type" OR by "Sport" (per wpmet.com)

#### Mobile Approach
- **Hamburger menu** with main top-level categories (MEN, WOMEN, KIDS, Sale, New & Trending)
- **Large category links** below the fold on mobile homepage as quick-entry shortcut (per econsultancy.com — "a smart move, given some may instinctively scroll, rather than heading for the burger menu")
- **Off-canvas or accordion pattern** for subcategory expansion (per creativecorner.studio)
- **Filter buttons** on mobile are smaller than Nike's — more fiddly (per econsultancy.com)
- **Filter menu issue:** Once open, cannot simply exit; must reload product selection (per econsultancy.com)

---

### 1.3 Decathlon

**Source:** Probe-Wren research, `megamenu-sports-retailers.md`

#### Levels Visible
- **Desktop: 2 levels visible** in the main navigation panel (category → subcategory). Deeper levels (3+) require clicking through to category landing pages, which reveal further subcategories via sidebar navigation ("Activities" sidebar).
- Decathlon does NOT show 3+ levels directly in the menu. They flatten to 2 levels max in the dropdown.
- Source: decathlon.com HTML structure analysis; aureatelabs.com CRO analysis (2024)

#### Column Layout
- **Mega menu is NOT used in the traditional sense.** Decathlon uses a search-navigation hybrid approach instead of a classic mega menu.
- On desktop, clicking a top-level category triggers a search-like overlay showing: (a) relevant subcategories as a structured list, (b) popular/featured products, (c) the search field auto-populated with the category name.
- Layout is a single-column list of subcategories + a product card section, not a multi-column grid.
- Source: hmmh.de/en/projects/decathlon-search-navigation

#### Images/Thumbnails
- **Yes** — subcategory landing pages show product thumbnails and category hero images. The search-navigation overlay shows product cards with images.
- Source: aureatelabs.com CRO analysis; decathlon.com HTML

#### Hover vs Click
- **Click to open.** The navigation is triggered by clicking a category link. It does NOT open on hover.
- The search-navigation system requires a deliberate click because it populates the search field and fetches results simultaneously.
- Source: hmmh.de case study: "Clicking on one of them makes it the first part of a search query"

#### Deep Category Handling
- Decathlon handles deep hierarchy by **delegating depth to category landing pages.** The main menu only shows 2 levels. Level 3+ is surfaced through:
  - **Category landing page** with a sidebar "Activities" navigation showing sibling/subsidiary categories
  - **Breadcrumbs** at the top of every category page
  - **Left-side filters** on PLPs for attributes (size, price, brand, color, etc.)
- Source: aureatelabs.com analysis: "sidebar navigation called 'Activities' provides additional browsing options"

#### Distinctive Patterns
1. **Search-Navigation Hybrid** — Categories integrated INTO the search experience. "Significantly more conversions" in A/B tests (hmmh case study).
2. **"Activities" Sidebar** — Persistent left sidebar on category pages showing related categories.
3. **Six quick-access categories** below the search bar.
4. **Vitamin Web design system** — Open-source design system with accordion and navigation components.
5. **No traditional mega menu** — Deliberately avoids a classic mega menu despite thousands of products.

#### Mobile Approach
- Hamburger menu (off-canvas drawer) with accordion-style expandable categories.
- Vitamin design system includes accordion components for mobile navigation.
- Search is prominently positioned at the top — reflects search-first philosophy.
- Breadcrumbs persist on mobile for orientation.

---

*End of Part 1 — continues in Part 2 (Foot Locker, JD Sports, ASOS, Zalando + comparison tables)*

<content>
1: # Mega Menu UX Research — Comprehensive Report for Athletica (Part 4: Mobile Strategy)
2: 
3: > **Compiled by:** Probe-Orion (Intelligence Team)
4: > **Task:** task-mega-menu-ux-001
5: > **Date:** 2026-07-19
6: > **Primary sources:** Probe-Sable, `megamenu-deep-hierarchy-part2.md` (Part B: Mobile Navigation)
7: 
8: ---
9: 
10: ## Section 3: Mobile Strategy
11: 
12: ### 3.1 Recommended Pattern: Hybrid Accordion + Drill-Down (Push Navigation)
13: 
14: **Primary recommendation: Accordion for Levels 1–2 → Switch to Drill-Down/Push navigation for Levels 3–5**
15: 
16: After extensive research of available patterns and competitor approaches, the recommended pattern for Athletica's 5-level hierarchy is a **hybrid accordion + drill-down system:**
17: 
18: - **Level 1 → Level 2:** Use an accordion pattern inside a full-screen overlay menu. Tapping a Level 1 category (e.g., "Boots") expands inline to show Level 2 brands (Nike, Adidas, Puma).
19: - **Level 2 → Level 3:** Tapping a Level 2 brand (e.g., "Nike") **triggers a push transition** to a new full-screen panel showing Level 3 models.
20: - **Level 3 → Level 4+:** Continue the drill-down/push pattern. Each tap pushes a new screen.
21: - **At any level:** A "View All [Category]" link and a prominent "Back" button (at the top) allow returning to parent levels.
22: 
23: Research-backed guidance:
24: - NN/g "Mobile Subnavigation" (2017): "Sequential menus" (drill-down) are recommended for deep hierarchies. Accordions work well when subcategories contain "less than 6" items. For more than 15 subcategories per primary category, use a category landing page.
25:   - Decision algorithm from NN/g: <6 subcategories → accordion/submenu; 6–15 subcategories → section menu; 15+ → category landing page
26:   - (Source: NN/g, "Mobile Subnavigation", Raluca Budiu, 2017, nngroup.com/articles/mobile-subnavigation/)
27: - NN/g "Menu-Design Checklist" (2024): Sequential navigation "can enable users to peruse a deep structure" and recommends it for deep hierarchies on mobile. Toyota's mobile site is cited as a good example. (Source: NN/g, 2024, guideline #9)
28: - Smashing Magazine (Vitaly Friedman, 2021): "Vertical accordions appear to be faster and more predictable than overlays (be it single-column or multiple layers). And split-menus appear to be faster and more predictable than accordions." Recommends starting with split-menus, then accordions, then overlays as complexity increases. (Source: Smashing Magazine, 2021)
29: - Boundev (2026): Recommends "Accordion Pattern" for 2–3 levels and "Drill-Down Pattern" for deeper levels. "Each level slides in as a full-screen panel, replacing the previous level. A back button or swipe gesture returns to the parent. Provides context for deep hierarchies without overwhelming the screen." (Source: Boundev, 2026)
30: 
31: ---
32: 
33: ### 3.2 Why This Works for 5 Levels
34: 
35: - **Levels 1–2 (Accordion):** Users can see all top-level categories at a glance (Boots, Clothing, Accessories). Expanding a category inline shows brands without losing context. This supports "sideways browsing" — jumping from one brand to another without going back to root.
36: - **Levels 3–5 (Drill-down/Push):** Once a user commits to a brand, push navigation gives them full-screen focus on that branch. Each level shows a clear "You are here" context via heading and back button. This avoids the "nested doll navigation" problem (NN/g term) where accordions become too deep and push content far down the screen.
37: - **Hybrid switch at Level 2:** Research shows accordions fail at depth because "the expanded ancestors of a deep-level category would push the current scope too far away from the top of the screen, thus requiring a lot of scrolling" (SGS case study, Smashing Magazine, 2016). Switching to push at Level 2 solves this.
38: - **NN/g decision algorithm applied:** Athletica's Level 1 categories likely contain 5-10 brand items at Level 2 — this falls in the accordion/submenu sweet spot (<6 recommended; 6-15 acceptable with section menu). Level 3+ models per brand may exceed 6 items, justifying the switch to drill-down/push.
39: 
40: ---
41: 
42: ### 3.3 Alternatives Considered
43: 
44: | Pattern | Pros | Cons | Verdict |
45: |---|---|---|---|
46: | **Pure Accordion (all 5 levels)** | Familiar pattern, users can see all levels expanded | 5 levels of indentation = loss of context, too much scrolling, "nested doll" problem (NN/g). SGS found 7 levels required 7 visual cues — impractical. | ❌ Rejected |
47: | **Pure Drill-Down/Push (all levels)** | Clear focus, works for any depth | No sideways browsing — users must go back to root to switch brands. NN/g warns "sequential menus can disorient users." | ⚠️ Works but loses overview |
48: | **Hamburger only** | Simple, standard | NN/g: "Hamburger menus hurt UX metrics" — discoverability cut ~50%. Users don't explore. | ❌ Rejected |
49: | **Section Menus** | Good for deep dives within one section | Only works if users stay in one section. Can't jump between different branches. | ⚠️ Rejected |
50: | **Category Landing Pages** | Always available, no interaction cost | Requires page load for every subcategory switch. High interaction cost. | ❌ Rejected |
51: | **Bottom Tab Bar (Level 1 only)** | Always visible, one-tap access | Only 3-5 items. Only covers top level. | ⚠️ Could supplement |
52: | **Hybrid Accordion + Drill-Down** | Best of both: overview + focus | Requires clear visual transition. Users need to learn two interaction patterns. | ✅ RECOMMENDED |
53: 
54: ---
55: 
56: ### 3.4 ASCII Wireframe Diagrams
57: 
58: #### Menu structure on mobile (initial state — full-screen overlay):
59: 
60: ```
61: ┌─────────────────────────────┐
62: │ ✕  Menu                  🔍 │  ← Header with close + search
63: ├─────────────────────────────┤
64: │                             │
65: │ ▶ Boots                     │  ← Level 1 (accordion)
66: │   ▶ Nike                    │  ← Level 2 expansions inline
67: │   ▶ Adidas                  │
68: │   ▶ Puma                    │
69: │   [View All Boots →]        │
70: │                             │
71: │ ▶ Clothing                  │  ← Another Level 1 accordion
72: │ ▶ Accessories               │
73: │ ▶ Sale                      │
74: │                             │
75: ├─────────────────────────────┤
76: │ [Brands] [Sports] [Help]    │  ← Utility links at bottom
77: └─────────────────────────────┘
78: ```
79: 
80: #### After tapping Level 2 (e.g., "Nike") — drill-down push screen:
81: 
82: ```
83: ┌─────────────────────────────┐
84: │ ← Back    Boots > Nike   🔍 │  ← Breadcrumb trail + back
85: ├─────────────────────────────┤
86: │                             │
87: │ ⚽ Nike Mercurial       →   │  ← Level 3 (drill-down list)
88: │ ⚽ Nike Phantom         →   │     Each with icon + arrow
89: │ ⚽ Nike Tiempo          →   │
90: │ ⚽ Nike Zoom            →   │
91: │                             │
92: │ [View All Nike Boots →]     │
93: │                             │
94: ├─────────────────────────────┤
95: │ 🔒 Member Access: Sign In   │
96: └─────────────────────────────┘
97: ```
98: 
99: #### After tapping Level 3 (e.g., "Mercurial") — further drill-down:
100: 
101: ```
102: ┌─────────────────────────────┐
103: │ ← Back    Nike > Mercurial  │
104: ├─────────────────────────────┤
105: │                             │
106: │ Superfly 9 Elite       →   │  ← Level 4 (sub-models)
107: │ Superfly 9 Pro         →   │
108: │ Superfly 9 Academy     →   │
109: │ Vapor 16 Elite         →   │
110: │ Vapor 16 Pro           →   │
111: │ Vapor 16 Academy       →   │
112: │                             │
113: │ [View All Mercurial →]      │
114: │                             │
115: └─────────────────────────────┘
116: ```
117: 
118: ---
119: 
120: ### 3.5 Implementation Guidance
121: 
122: 1. **Full-screen overlay:** Use a slide-in drawer (left side) that takes over the full viewport. Do NOT use a partial overlay — users need the full screen to see deep hierarchy.
123: 
124: 2. **Animated transitions:** Use CSS transforms for push transitions (slide left). Duration: 200–300ms. (Source: SGS case study used 300ms horizontal slide)
125: 
126: 3. **Breadcrumb trail:** Always show current path at the top (e.g., "Boots > Nike > Mercurial"). NN/g emphasizes orienting users in deep hierarchies. (Source: NN/g, "Mobile Subnavigation", 2017)
127: 
128: 4. **"View All" links at each level:** Every level should have a prominent "View All [Category]" link at the bottom. Baymard: "Have a 'View All' option in the main navigation at each level of the mobile product catalog — only 24% get it right." (Source: Baymard)
129: 
130: 5. **Touch targets:** 44×44px minimum for all items. Indentation for hierarchy: 16–20px per level. (Source: NN/g touch target guidelines; Boundev)
131: 
132: 6. **Icons:** Use chevron-right (→) for items that drill down (levels 3+). Use chevron-down (▼) for accordions (levels 1–2). Keep icons consistent. (Source: Smashing Magazine, 2022)
133: 
134: 7. **Color/indentation hierarchy:** Use distinct visual cues for each level. Smashing Magazine warns: "7 levels of navigation requires 7 degrees of visual cue" — impractical. Keep to 2–3 visual styles maximum. (Source: SGS case study, 2016)
135: 
136: 8. **Performance:** Conditionally load deeper navigation branches. SGS loaded first 3 levels in HTML by default, then loaded deeper branches via JavaScript on user intent. (Source: Smashing Magazine SGS case study, 2016)
137: 
138: 9. **Search bar:** Persistent at the top of the mobile nav overlay (inspired by Decathlon's search-first approach per hmmh.de case study).
139: 
140: 10. **Animation:** Nike-style staggered fade-in (~50ms per item) for accordion reveals. CSS transform slide for drill-down transitions. (Source: muffingroup.com; SGS case study)
141: 
142: ---
143: 
144: ### 3.6 Competitor Comparison Table
145: 
146: | Site | Mobile Nav Pattern | Levels Shown | Notes |
147: |---|---|---|---|
148: | **Nike** | Hamburger → Accordion (L1–L2) → Drill-down (L3+) | 3 levels in menu, defer to PLP | Clean separation: accordion for categories, push for deeper. Top 1% Baymard performer. |
149: | **Adidas** | Hamburger → Accordion (all levels) | 3 levels in menu | Less scannable than Nike. Bold typefaces for main categories. |
150: | **ASOS** | Bottom nav + Hamburger for categories | 2 levels in hamburger, defer to PLP | Unique bottom tab approach. Categories in full-screen overlay with images. |
151: | **Zalando** | Hamburger → Accordion (1 level) → Links | 2 levels in menu | Minimal — most navigation deferred to PLP. Text-only subcategories. |
152: | **Decathlon** | Hamburger → Accordion (3+ levels) | 3+ levels | Handles deep sports hierarchy. Uses icons and thumbnails. |
153: | **Foot Locker** | Hamburger → Drill-down (all levels) | 3+ levels | Push navigation for all levels. Brand-first approach. Top 1% Baymard performer. |
154: | **Target** | Full-screen overlay → Click-only, one column | 2–3 levels | Smashing Magazine praises Target: "avoids multi-column layout, shows one level at a time on tap/click." |
155: 
156: **Key competitor insight:** Nike and Foot Locker (both Top 1% Baymard performers) use a **hybrid approach**: accordion for initial levels, drill-down for deeper levels. This validates the recommended pattern for Athletica.
157: 
158: ---
159: 
160: ### 3.7 Accessibility Considerations — Mobile
161: 
162: 1. **Keyboard navigation:** Full keyboard support — Tab, Arrow keys, Enter/Space, Escape. (Source: Boundev, 2026; WCAG 2.1 AA)
163: 2. **Screen readers:** Use `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls` for accordion items. Use `aria-current="page"` for current category. (Source: Boundev, 2026)
164: 3. **Motion sensitivity:** Provide `prefers-reduced-motion` support — disable slide animations. (Source: WCAG 2.1 — 2.3.3)
165: 4. **Touch targets:** Minimum 44×44px, ideally 48×48dp (Material Design 3). (Source: NN/g; Material Design 3)
166: 5. **Focus management:** On drill-down push, move focus to panel heading. On close, return focus to trigger. (Source: WCAG 2.1 — 2.4.3)

display.text:
# Mega Menu UX Research — Comprehensive Report for Athletica (Part 4: Mobile Strategy)

> **Compiled by:** Probe-Orion (Intelligence Team)
> **Task:** task-mega-menu-ux-001
> **Date:** 2026-07-19
> **Primary sources:** Probe-Sable, `megamenu-deep-hierarchy-part2.md` (Part B: Mobile Navigation)

---

## Section 3: Mobile Strategy

### 3.1 Recommended Pattern: Hybrid Accordion + Drill-Down (Push Navigation)

**Primary recommendation: Accordion for Levels 1–2 → Switch to Drill-Down/Push navigation for Levels 3–5**

After extensive research of available patterns and competitor approaches, the recommended pattern for Athletica's 5-level hierarchy is a **hybrid accordion + drill-down system:**

- **Level 1 → Level 2:** Use an accordion pattern inside a full-screen overlay menu. Tapping a Level 1 category (e.g., "Boots") expands inline to show Level 2 brands (Nike, Adidas, Puma).
- **Level 2 → Level 3:** Tapping a Level 2 brand (e.g., "Nike") **triggers a push transition** to a new full-screen panel showing Level 3 models.
- **Level 3 → Level 4+:** Continue the drill-down/push pattern. Each tap pushes a new screen.
- **At any level:** A "View All [Category]" link and a prominent "Back" button (at the top) allow returning to parent levels.

Research-backed guidance:
- NN/g "Mobile Subnavigation" (2017): "Sequential menus" (drill-down) are recommended for deep hierarchies. Accordions work well when subcategories contain "less than 6" items. For more than 15 subcategories per primary category, use a category landing page.
  - Decision algorithm from NN/g: <6 subcategories → accordion/submenu; 6–15 subcategories → section menu; 15+ → category landing page
  - (Source: NN/g, "Mobile Subnavigation", Raluca Budiu, 2017, nngroup.com/articles/mobile-subnavigation/)
- NN/g "Menu-Design Checklist" (2024): Sequential navigation "can enable users to peruse a deep structure" and recommends it for deep hierarchies on mobile. Toyota's mobile site is cited as a good example. (Source: NN/g, 2024, guideline #9)
- Smashing Magazine (Vitaly Friedman, 2021): "Vertical accordions appear to be faster and more predictable than overlays (be it single-column or multiple layers). And split-menus appear to be faster and more predictable than accordions." Recommends starting with split-menus, then accordions, then overlays as complexity increases. (Source: Smashing Magazine, 2021)
- Boundev (2026): Recommends "Accordion Pattern" for 2–3 levels and "Drill-Down Pattern" for deeper levels. "Each level slides in as a full-screen panel, replacing the previous level. A back button or swipe gesture returns to the parent. Provides context for deep hierarchies without overwhelming the screen." (Source: Boundev, 2026)

---

### 3.2 Why This Works for 5 Levels

- **Levels 1–2 (Accordion):** Users can see all top-level categories at a glance (Boots, Clothing, Accessories). Expanding a category inline shows brands without losing context. This supports "sideways browsing" — jumping from one brand to another without going back to root.
- **Levels 3–5 (Drill-down/Push):** Once a user commits to a brand, push navigation gives them full-screen focus on that branch. Each level shows a clear "You are here" context via heading and back button. This avoids the "nested doll navigation" problem (NN/g term) where accordions become too deep and push content far down the screen.
- **Hybrid switch at Level 2:** Research shows accordions fail at depth because "the expanded ancestors of a deep-level category would push the current scope too far away from the top of the screen, thus requiring a lot of scrolling" (SGS case study, Smashing Magazine, 2016). Switching to push at Level 2 solves this.
- **NN/g decision algorithm applied:** Athletica's Level 1 categories likely contain 5-10 brand items at Level 2 — this falls in the accordion/submenu sweet spot (<6 recommended; 6-15 acceptable with section menu). Level 3+ models per brand may exceed 6 items, justifying the switch to drill-down/push.

---

### 3.3 Alternatives Considered

| Pattern | Pros | Cons | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Pure Accordion (all 5 levels)** | Familiar pattern, users can see all levels expanded | 5 levels of indentation = loss of context, too much scrolling, "nested doll" problem (NN/g). SGS found 7 levels required 7 visual cues — impractical. | ❌ Rejected |
| **Pure Drill-Down/Push (all levels)** | Clear focus, works for any depth | No sideways browsing — users must go back to root to switch brands. NN/g warns "sequential menus can disorient users." | ⚠️ Works but loses overview |
| **Hamburger only** | Simple, standard | NN/g: "Hamburger menus hurt UX metrics" — discoverability cut ~50%. Users don't explore. | ❌ Rejected |
| **Section Menus** | Good for deep dives within one section | Only works if users stay in one section. Can't jump between different branches. | ⚠️ Rejected |
| **Category Landing Pages** | Always available, no interaction cost | Requires page load for every subcategory switch. High interaction cost. | ❌ Rejected |
| **Bottom Tab Bar (Level 1 only)** | Always visible, one-tap access | Only 3-5 items. Only covers top level. | ⚠️ Could supplement |
| **Hybrid Accordion + Drill-Down** | Best of both: overview + focus | Requires clear visual transition. Users need to learn two interaction patterns. | ✅ RECOMMENDED |

---

### 3.4 ASCII Wireframe Diagrams

#### Menu structure on mobile (initial state — full-screen overlay):

```
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│ ✕  Menu                  🔍 │  ← Header with close + search
├─────────────────────────────┤
│                             │
│ ▶ Boots                     │  ← Level 1 (accordion)
│   ▶ Nike                    │  ← Level 2 expansions inline
│   ▶ Adidas                  │
│   ▶ Puma                    │
│   [View All Boots →]        │
│                             │
│ ▶ Clothing                  │  ← Another Level 1 accordion
│ ▶ Accessories               │
│ ▶ Sale                      │
│                             │
├─────────────────────────────┤
│ [Brands] [Sports] [Help]    │  ← Utility links at bottom
└─────────────────────────────┘
```

#### After tapping Level 2 (e.g., "Nike") — drill-down push screen:

```
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│ ← Back    Boots > Nike   🔍 │  ← Breadcrumb trail + back
├─────────────────────────────┤
│                             │
│ ⚽ Nike Mercurial       →   │  ← Level 3 (drill-down list)
│ ⚽ Nike Phantom         →   │     Each with icon + arrow
│ ⚽ Nike Tiempo          →   │
│ ⚽ Nike Zoom            →   │
│                             │
│ [View All Nike Boots →]     │
│                             │
├─────────────────────────────┤
│ 🔒 Member Access: Sign In   │
└─────────────────────────────┘
```

#### After tapping Level 3 (e.g., "Mercurial") — further drill-down:

```
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│ ← Back    Nike > Mercurial  │
├─────────────────────────────┤
│                             │
│ Superfly 9 Elite       →   │  ← Level 4 (sub-models)
│ Superfly 9 Pro         →   │
│ Superfly 9 Academy     →   │
│ Vapor 16 Elite         →   │
│ Vapor 16 Pro           →   │
│ Vapor 16 Academy       →   │
│                             │
│ [View All Mercurial →]      │
│                             │
└─────────────────────────────┘
```

---

### 3.5 Implementation Guidance

1. **Full-screen overlay:** Use a slide-in drawer (left side) that takes over the full viewport. Do NOT use a partial overlay — users need the full screen to see deep hierarchy.

2. **Animated transitions:** Use CSS transforms for push transitions (slide left). Duration: 200–300ms. (Source: SGS case study used 300ms horizontal slide)

3. **Breadcrumb trail:** Always show current path at the top (e.g., "Boots > Nike > Mercurial"). NN/g emphasizes orienting users in deep hierarchies. (Source: NN/g, "Mobile Subnavigation", 2017)

4. **"View All" links at each level:** Every level should have a prominent "View All [Category]" link at the bottom. Baymard: "Have a 'View All' option in the main navigation at each level of the mobile product catalog — only 24% get it right." (Source: Baymard)

5. **Touch targets:** 44×44px minimum for all items. Indentation for hierarchy: 16–20px per level. (Source: NN/g touch target guidelines; Boundev)

6. **Icons:** Use chevron-right (→) for items that drill down (levels 3+). Use chevron-down (▼) for accordions (levels 1–2). Keep icons consistent. (Source: Smashing Magazine, 2022)

7. **Color/indentation hierarchy:** Use distinct visual cues for each level. Smashing Magazine warns: "7 levels of navigation requires 7 degrees of visual cue" — impractical. Keep to 2–3 visual styles maximum. (Source: SGS case study, 2016)

8. **Performance:** Conditionally load deeper navigation branches. SGS loaded first 3 levels in HTML by default, then loaded deeper branches via JavaScript on user intent. (Source: Smashing Magazine SGS case study, 2016)

9. **Search bar:** Persistent at the top of the mobile nav overlay (inspired by Decathlon's search-first approach per hmmh.de case study).

10. **Animation:** Nike-style staggered fade-in (~50ms per item) for accordion reveals. CSS transform slide for drill-down transitions. (Source: muffingroup.com; SGS case study)

---

### 3.6 Competitor Comparison Table

| Site | Mobile Nav Pattern | Levels Shown | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Nike** | Hamburger → Accordion (L1–L2) → Drill-down (L3+) | 3 levels in menu, defer to PLP | Clean separation: accordion for categories, push for deeper. Top 1% Baymard performer. |
| **Adidas** | Hamburger → Accordion (all levels) | 3 levels in menu | Less scannable than Nike. Bold typefaces for main categories. |
| **ASOS** | Bottom nav + Hamburger for categories | 2 levels in hamburger, defer to PLP | Unique bottom tab approach. Categories in full-screen overlay with images. |
| **Zalando** | Hamburger → Accordion (1 level) → Links | 2 levels in menu | Minimal — most navigation deferred to PLP. Text-only subcategories. |
| **Decathlon** | Hamburger → Accordion (3+ levels) | 3+ levels | Handles deep sports hierarchy. Uses icons and thumbnails. |
| **Foot Locker** | Hamburger → Drill-down (all levels) | 3+ levels | Push navigation for all levels. Brand-first approach. Top 1% Baymard performer. |
| **Target** | Full-screen overlay → Click-only, one column | 2–3 levels | Smashing Magazine praises Target: "avoids multi-column layout, shows one level at a time on tap/click." |

**Key competitor insight:** Nike and Foot Locker (both Top 1% Baymard performers) use a **hybrid approach**: accordion for initial levels, drill-down for deeper levels. This validates the recommended pattern for Athletica.

---

### 3.7 Accessibility Considerations — Mobile

1. **Keyboard navigation:** Full keyboard support — Tab, Arrow keys, Enter/Space, Escape. (Source: Boundev, 2026; WCAG 2.1 AA)
2. **Screen readers:** Use `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls` for accordion items. Use `aria-current="page"` for current category. (Source: Boundev, 2026)
3. **Motion sensitivity:** Provide `prefers-reduced-motion` support — disable slide animations. (Source: WCAG 2.1 — 2.3.3)
4. **Touch targets:** Minimum 44×44px, ideally 48×48dp (Material Design 3). (Source: NN/g; Material Design 3)
5. **Focus management:** On drill-down push, move focus to panel heading. On close, return focus to trigger. (Source: WCAG 2.1 — 2.4.3)
6. **Contrast:** All text must meet WCAG AA (4.5:1 normal, 3:1 large text). (Source: NN/g, 2017)
7. **Orientation:** Support portrait and landscape. In landscape, consider split-menu showing two levels. (Source: Smashing Magazine, 2022)
8. **Back button behavior:** Use breadcrumb-style back ("← Back to [Parent]"), not generic "Back." Avoid confusion with browser back button. (Source: NN/g, "Mobile Subnavigation", 2017)

---

### Summary: Key Mobile Decisions for Athletica

| Decision | Recommendation | Primary Source |
|---|---|---|
| Mobile pattern | Hybrid accordion (L1–L2) + drill-down (L3–L5) | NN/g, Boundev |
| Accordion depth | Switch at Level 2 (≤6 items per group) | NN/g (<6 = accordion) |
| Touch targets | 44×44px minimum | NN/g, Material Design 3 |
| Performance | Load L1–L3 in HTML, lazy-load deeper | SGS case study |
| "View All" links | At every level | Baymard (only 24% do this) |
| Breadcrumbs | Always show path at top | NN/g "Mobile Subnavigation" |
| Animations | Accordion: staggered fade (50ms/item); Push: 200-300ms slide | Muffingroup.com; SGS case study |

---

*End of Part 4 — continues in Part 5 (Athletica-Specific Recommendations + Sources Cited)*

# Mega Menu UX Research — Comprehensive Report for Athletica (Part 5: Athletica-Specific Recommendations)

> **Compiled by:** Probe-Orion (Intelligence Team)
> **Task:** task-mega-menu-ux-001
> **Date:** 2026-07-19
> **Synthesis from ALL input files.** Unresolved items marked `[NOT FOUND — ask CEO]`.

---

## Section 4: Athletica-Specific Recommendations

### 4.1 Recommended Desktop Mega Menu Wireframe

#### Top-Level Nav Bar
- **Level 1 categories** as text links: `Boots | Clothing | Equipment | Accessories | Brands | Sale`
- **Inspiration:** Nike's ~6-item top-level nav (per styles.refero.design); JD Sports' consistent template (per Richard Ilott's redesign)
- **Audience-first split?** `[NOT FOUND — ask CEO]` — decide if splitting by Gender (Men's/Women's) or Category first

#### Mega Menu Panel (4-Column Layout)

Wireframe when hovering/clicking "Boots":

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ [Boots] [Clothing] [Equipment] [Accessories] [Brands] [Sale]     │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                  │
│  COLUMN 1          │  COLUMN 2       │  COLUMN 3       │ COL 4   │
│  CATEGORY + EDITS  │  BRANDS         │  MODELS         │ FEATURED│
│                    │  (48px logos)   │  (60px thumbs)  │         │
│                    │                 │                 │         │
│  ▶ All Boots       │ [Nike logo]     │ [img]           │ [img]   │
│                    │   Nike          │   Mercurial     │         │
│  Edits:            │                 │   Phantom       │ Latest  │
│  › New In          │ [Adidas logo]   │   Tiempo        │ Release │
│  › Best Sellers    │   Adidas        │   X             │         │
│  › By Surface      │                 │   Predator      │         │
│    - FG            │ [Puma logo]     │                 │ [CTA:   │
│    - AG            │   Puma          │ [img]           │ Shop →] │
│    - TF            │   Ultra         │   Future 7      │         │
│    - SG            │                 │   King          │         │
│                    │                 │                 │         │
│                    │ [New Balance]   │ [img]           │         │
│                    │ [Mizuno]        │   Fresh Foam    │         │
│                    │                 │   Tekela        │         │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  [View All Boots →]          │  [View All Brands →]              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

#### Column Descriptions

**Column 1 — Category links + Edits (Level 1)**
- "All Boots" as clickable heading → full Boots category page
- Curated "Edits": New In, Best Sellers, By Surface (FG, AG, TF, SG)
- Inspired by JD Sports' "Edits" column (per Richard Ilott's redesign) and Nike's "New & Featured" column
- "By Surface" is Athletica-specific — a unique differentiator for football boots

**Column 2 — Brand links with 48px logos (Level 2)**
- Each brand with a small logo (48×48px) before the name
- Brands: Nike, Adidas, Puma, New Balance, Mizuno, Umbro, etc.
- Inspired by Foot Locker's "Brands" column and JD Sports' brand column (per Probe-Wren)
- Logo size per Probe-Sable recommendation (Part A, §A4): "brand thumbs at 48px"
- Source: NN/g "visual cues for long menus" (2024); Baymard: thumbnails reduce hesitation (2025)

**Column 3 — Model links with 60px thumbnails (Level 3)**
- Each model with a small product thumbnail (60×60px)
- Top models per brand (Nike: Mercurial, Phantom, Tiempo, Zoom)
- Thumbnails at 60px per Probe-Sable (Part A, §A4)
- Vertical scroll if model list exceeds available space

**Column 4 — Featured/promotional column**
- Latest release spotlight with product image
- "Shop All [Category]" CTA button
- Single image only — no carousel, auto-play, or complex widgets
- Inspired by JD Sports' `nav-promotions` section and Nike's promo image block
- Source: NN/g warns against "GUI widgets" — keep to single CTA (per "Mega Menus Work Well", 2017)

**Bottom row:**
- "View All Boots" (left) — inspired by Adidas's bold "All" links (per econsultancy.com)
- "View All Brands" (right)
- Full-width, subtle visual separator

#### Hover/Click Behavior
- **Primary: Click to open** — consistent across devices (per NN/g guideline #13, 2024)
- **Secondary: Hover with 400ms delay** — for mouse users (per Baymard 300-500ms recommendation)
- **Amazon triangle technique** — trajectory triangle prevents accidental closes during diagonal movement (per bjk5.com)
- **Exit delay:** 500ms minimum before menu closes (per NN/g, "Mega Menus Work Well", 2017)
- **Close:** Click outside panel or Escape key

#### Scrolling
- Mega menu panel scrolls vertically if content exceeds viewport height
- No horizontal scroll within mega menu
- Source: Boundev (2026)

#### Cutoff
- Mega menu shows Levels 1-3
- Levels 4-5 handled via PLP filters + breadcrumbs
- Each Level 3 link → intermediary PLP: `/boots/nike/mercurial/`
- On PLP: Level 4 sub-models as filterable groups, Level 5 as filter facets
- Source: NN/g guideline #14 (2024); SGS case study (2016)

---

### 4.2 Athletica's 5-Level Hierarchy Mapping

| Mega Menu Location | Level | Example | Handled By |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Top-level nav bar** | Level 1: Category | "Boots" | Mega menu (text link) |
| **Column 2** | Level 2: Brand | "Nike", "Adidas", "Puma" | Mega menu (48px logos) |
| **Column 3** | Level 3: Model | "Mercurial", "Phantom" | Mega menu (60px thumbs) |
| **PLP Filters** | Level 4: Sub-model | "Vapor 16 Elite" | PLP faceted filters |
| **PLP Filters** | Level 5: Product Type | "FG", "AG", "TF", "SG" | PLP filter chips |

**Key design decisions:**

1. **Levels 1-3 in mega menu** — NN/g: mega menus "can support 2–3 tiers" (per "Menu-Design Checklist", 2024)

2. **Level 4-5 on PLP** — Decathlon's "Activities" sidebar pattern applies here (per aureatelabs.com)

3. **Breadcrumbs on PLP** — show full path: `Boots > Nike > Mercurial > Vapor 16 Elite > FG`

4. **Left sidebar on PLP** — sibling sub-models and parent categories (inspired by Nike's nested sidebar, per econsultancy.com)

5. **PLP URL structure** — `/boots/nike/mercurial/?stud=fg` or similar

---

### 4.3 Recommended Mobile Navigation

#### Structure
- **Hamburger icon** → opens **full-screen overlay**
- **Accordion for Level 1→2:** Tapping "Boots" expands inline to show brands
- **Push/drill-down for Level 2→3+:** Tapping "Nike" pushes a new screen showing models
- **Breadcrumb trail** at top of each drill-down screen (e.g., "Boots > Nike")
- **"View All" link** at every level
- **Search bar** persistent at top of nav overlay

#### Inspiration
- **Full-screen overlay:** Nike (per muffingroup.com)
- **Drill-down for deeper levels:** Foot Locker (Top 1% Baymard performer) + ASOS
- **Hybrid accordion + drill-down switch at Level 2:** Probe-Sable per NN/g + Boundev
- **Search-first approach:** Decathlon (per hmmh.de — "significantly more conversions")
- **"View All" links:** "Baymard: only 24% get it right" — high-impact, low-effort

#### Wireframe — Initial State

```
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│ ✕  Menu                  🔍 │
├─────────────────────────────┤
│ ▶ Boots                     │  ← Tap to expand accordion
│ ▶ Clothing                  │
│ ▶ Equipment                 │
│ ▶ Accessories               │
│ ▶ Sale                      │
├─────────────────────────────┤
│ [Brands] [Sports] [Help]    │
└─────────────────────────────┘
```

#### Wireframe — Accordion Expanded (Level 1→2)

```
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│ ✕  Menu                  🔍 │
├─────────────────────────────┤
│ ▼ Boots                     │  ← Expanded
│   ▶ All Boots               │     (→ = PLP link)
│   ▶ New In                  │
│   ▶ Best Sellers            │
│   ▶ Nike  →                 │     (→ = drill-down)
│   ▶ Adidas →                │
│   ▶ Puma  →                 │
│   ▶ View All Brands →       │
│ ▶ Clothing                  │  ← Collapsed below
│ ▶ Equipment                 │
│ ▶ Accessories               │
│ ▶ Sale                      │
└─────────────────────────────┘
```

#### Wireframe — Drill-Down (Level 3: Models)

```
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│ ← Back    Boots > Nike   🔍 │
├─────────────────────────────┤
│ ⚽ Nike Mercurial       →   │
│ ⚽ Nike Phantom         →   │
│ ⚽ Nike Tiempo          →   │
│ ⚽ Nike Zoom            →   │
│ [View All Nike Boots →]     │
└─────────────────────────────┘
```

#### Wireframe — Further Drill-Down (Level 4: Sub-models)

```
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│ ← Back    Nike > Mercurial  │
├─────────────────────────────┤
│ Superfly 9 Elite       →   │
│ Superfly 9 Pro         →   │
│ Superfly 9 Academy     →   │
│ Vapor 16 Elite         →   │
│ Vapor 16 Pro           →   │
│ Vapor 16 Academy       →   │
│ [View All Mercurial →]      │
└─────────────────────────────┘
```

---

### 4.4 Why This Layout Works for 5 Levels

1. **NN/g finding:** Mega menus "can support 2–3 tiers" (per "Menu-Design Checklist", 2024). Athletica shows Levels 1-3.

2. **Baymard finding:** Users overwhelmed beyond ~10 options per level (2025). 4-column layout chunks into manageable groups.

3. **Decathlon's search-nav hybrid:** "Significantly more conversions" (per hmmh.de). Integrate search with menu.

4. **Nike's audience-first approach:** Segments massive catalog (per exclusiveaddons.com, wpmet.com). Consider gender-first if applicable.

5. **Adidas's dual-dimension navigation:** Browse by Product Type AND by Sport (per wpmet.com). "By Surface" column adapts this for football boots.

6. **JD Sports' consistent template:** Same structure across all categories (per Richard Ilott). Apply 4-column template consistently.

7. **SGS 7-level case study:** Load L1-L3 in HTML, lazy-load deeper via JS (per Smashing Magazine, 2016). Apply this performance pattern.

8. **Foot Locker's Brand-as-column:** Validated by a Top 1% Baymard performer. Directly applicable since Level 2 = Brand.

9. **Nike + Foot Locker (Top 1% Baymard):** Both use hybrid accordion + drill-down on mobile (per Probe-Sable Part B). Validates the mobile pattern.

10. **Zalando's early segmentation:** Cookie-based preference skips re-selection (per happycoding). Apply Hick's Law — store user preferences.

---

*Continues in Part 6 (Unresolved Items + Sources Cited)*

### Deliverables — You Must Return ALL 5

#### 1. ANALYSIS: How the Current Implementation Works
- Explain the current `buildColumns()` algorithm (the 5-slot column packing logic with level-based nesting)

- How does it handle the 11 categories?

#### 2. GAP ANALYSIS: Current vs Best Practices
Compare current MegaMenu.tsx against the research findings from parts 1-6:
- **Column structure:** Research recommends 4-column layout (Category Edit links | Brands with logos | Models with thumbnails | Featured). Current uses variable-width columns with 5-slot packing. What's the gap?

- **Hover/click behavior:** Research recommends click-to-open primary + hover with 400ms delay. Current? (check if it's hover-only or click)
- **Mobile:** Research recommends hybrid accordion (L1-L2) + drill-down (L3-L5). Current? (check if mobile exists)
- **11 categories:** Research recommends max 6 top-level items. Current has 11. How to handle? (More dropdown? Featured only?)

#### 3. EXAMPLES FROM REAL SITES
Synthesize from the existing research files the key examples showing the "category column with nested brands/models" pattern:
- **JD Sports** — consistent 6-column template (Edits → Footwear → Clothing → Accessories → Brands → Collections)

- **Cutoff:** 3 levels in menu, Levels 4-5 handled via PLP filters
- **Mobile wireframe:** Hamburger → full-screen overlay. Accordion for L1→L2. Push/drill-down for L2→L3+. Breadcrumb trail at top. "View All" links at each level. Search bar persistent.
